academicTalks.transcript: Today I want to talk about peer mentoring programs and how they affect whether first-year students stay enrolled. In a peer mentoring program, a returning student—usually in their second or third year—is paired with an incoming first-year student to offer guidance on things like choosing classes, finding study groups, and adjusting to campus life. Several universities have tracked retention, meaning how many students return for a second year, comparing students who were paired with a mentor to those who weren't. Across multiple campuses, first-year students with a mentor returned at noticeably higher rates than students without one. Researchers point to two likely reasons. First, mentors help students solve small problems—like navigating financial aid forms—before those problems become reasons to leave. Second, having one dedicated point of contact seems to reduce the sense of isolation that many first-year students report, especially in their first few months. It's worth noting that mentoring seems to matter most for students living far from home, where that built-in support network is otherwise missing entirely.

How class schedules are assigned to first-year students
How universities select mentors for programs
How financial aid forms are processed

questions.explanationZh: 講者一開始說明主題是「peer mentoring programs and how they affect whether first-year students stay enrolled」；其餘選項提到選拔導師、財務表格處理、排課，原文均未提及主旨。

questions.stem: According to the talk, what does a peer mentor typically help with?

options.text: Choosing classes and adjusting to campus life
Grading first-year students' course assignments
Approving students' financial aid applications
Assigning first-year students to dorm rooms

questions.explanationZh: 講者提到導師協助「choosing classes, finding study groups, and adjusting to campus life」；其餘選項提到批改作業、宿舍分配、核准助學金，原文皆未提及。

They take more difficult courses
They otherwise lack a built-in support network

academicTalks.transcript: Let's look at how flexible shift scheduling affects employee turnover in retail companies. Turnover here just means how often employees quit and need to be replaced. Traditionally, retail shifts are assigned by managers with little employee input, which can clash with school schedules, childcare, or second jobs. Some retail chains have started letting employees submit preferred shift windows and swap shifts directly with coworkers through an app. Researchers compared turnover rates at stores before and after this kind of flexible scheduling was introduced. Stores that adopted flexible scheduling saw turnover drop by roughly a quarter within the first year. Exit interviews with employees who left the traditional stores often cited scheduling conflicts as a major reason for quitting, even more often than pay. Interestingly, the effect was strongest among part-time employees juggling multiple commitments, since they benefited most from being able to trade shifts without needing manager approval each time. Full-time employees showed a smaller, though still positive, change in turnover, suggesting flexible scheduling helps every worker but especially those balancing several roles.

questions.stem: What is this talk mainly about?

options.text: How retail companies set and periodically revise employee pay structures
How new retail store managers are trained and evaluated
How customer satisfaction surveys are collected in retail chains
Flexible shift scheduling and retail employee turnover

academicTalks.transcript: Today's topic is participatory budgeting, a process where residents vote directly on how a portion of a city's budget gets spent, rather than leaving every decision to elected officials alone. Typically, a city sets aside a fixed amount—often a small percentage of the total budget—and residents propose and then vote on specific projects, like repairing a playground or adding streetlights to a dark intersection. Cities that have adopted participatory budgeting over the past decade show a consistent pattern: spending shifts noticeably toward small, neighborhood-level projects rather than large citywide infrastructure. Before participatory budgeting, most discretionary funds went to larger projects chosen by city planners, which sometimes overlooked smaller but urgently needed repairs in specific neighborhoods. Once residents vote directly, projects like sidewalk repairs, community garden funding, and park benches tend to win more often than they would under a traditional budget process. Planners see this less as residents ignoring the bigger picture and more as residents having direct knowledge of problems that citywide planning sometimes misses entirely.

academicTalks.transcript: Why are small daily routines easier to stick with than big lifestyle overhauls? Psychologists have studied this by comparing two groups: one group tries to adopt one small daily habit, like a five-minute walk after lunch, while another group commits to a much larger change, like a complete diet and exercise overhaul starting all at once. Using habit-tracking apps, researchers followed both groups over several months. The small-habit group showed dramatically higher completion rates—people kept doing their five-minute walk long after the large-change group had mostly abandoned their bigger plans. One explanation is that small habits require very little willpower, so they survive busy or stressful days when motivation is low. Large overhauls, by contrast, depend on consistently high motivation every single day, and even one missed day can feel like total failure, which often leads people to quit entirely rather than just skip a day and continue. Researchers also found that small habits tend to naturally expand over time—people who stuck with the short walk often added other small changes later, building up gradually instead of all at once.

questions.stem: What is the main point of this talk?

options.text: Missing even one day guarantees people will quit their routine
Small habits are easier to maintain than big lifestyle changes
Habit-tracking apps are the most reliable way to measure success

questions.explanationZh: 講者主旨為「small habits are easier to maintain than large overhauls」；(b)僅為支持性解釋而非主旨、(c)原文未評價APP可靠性、(d)過度推論「一天沒做就放棄」為必然結果，原文僅稱這種情況「常導致」放棄，非絕對。

options.text: By surveying participants' friends and family
